procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amravati
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 08.12.2022 of the High Court of Andhra Pradesh at Amravati in WP No. 36742 of 2022.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The detenu's brother-in-law approached the High Court by way of a writ of Habeas Corpus contending that the continued detention of the detenu after the grant of remission was illegal. The High Court accepted the contention and allowed the writ petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Andhra Pradesh appealed the High Court's order to the Supreme Court, challenging the High Court's decision to allow the writ petition and order the detenu's release. The Supreme Court dismissed the appeal, upholding the High Court's decision.

directions: The detenu shall be set at liberty forthwith.

issue.issue_text: Whether the continued detention of the detenu after the grant of remission in the first case was illegal.

facts: The detenu was serving a life sentence for a murder conviction from 2006.
He was also convicted in a separate case for kidnapping and sentenced to one year of simple imprisonment.
During his incarceration, the detenu escaped from custody twice but was recaptured.
The government granted the detenu special remission in his life sentence case, ordering his release.
However, he was not released. The State argued that his one-year sentence for kidnapping should only begin after the remission of his life sentence was granted.
law: Section 426(2)(b) of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.) states that for an escaped convict, a subsequent sentence shall begin only after the convict has served the unexpired portion of their former sentence.

Section 427(2) of the Cr.P.C. states that when a person already serving a life sentence is subsequently sentenced to another term of imprisonment, the subsequent sentence shall run concurrently with the life sentence.
application: The Court first considered the State's argument that Section 426(2)(b) should apply because the detenu was an escaped convict.

However, the Court identified a legal problem with applying this section to a life convict. It reasoned that a life sentence is for the convict's entire natural life, and therefore, in a technical legal sense, there is no 'unexpired' portion of the sentence. Remission is an executive act of grace, but it does not change the fact that the sentence itself is for life.
Because Section 426(2)(b) was found to be inapplicable to a life convict, the Court determined that Section 427(2) was the correct provision to apply.
According to Section 427(2), the one-year sentence for kidnapping must run concurrently (at the same time) with the life sentence for murder.
Since the detenu had been serving his life sentence since 2006, the one-year concurrent sentence for kidnapping had already been completed long before the remission was granted.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the continued detention of the detenu was illegal. It held that the one-year sentence for kidnapping ran concurrently with the life sentence and had already been served. Therefore, the Court upheld the High Court's decision, dismissed the State's appeal, and ordered that the detenu be set at liberty immediately.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court's application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. to the case was in order.

facts: A person (detenu) was serving a life sentence for a murder conviction from 2006.
Subsequently, the detenu was also convicted for kidnapping and sentenced to one year of simple imprisonment.
The text notes that the case involves an "escaped convict."
The government granted remission for the life sentence, but prison authorities refused to release the detenu.
The authorities argued that the one-year sentence for kidnapping should only begin after the remission of the life sentence.
The High Court, in a habeas corpus petition, ruled that the continued detention was illegal and ordered the detenu's release, prompting the State to appeal to the Supreme Court.
law: Section 426(2)(b) Cr.P.C. deals with escaped convicts and states that a subsequent sentence shall take effect only after the convict has served the unexpired portion of their former sentence.

Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. states that when a person already undergoing a life sentence is subsequently sentenced to a term of imprisonment, the subsequent sentence must run concurrently with the life sentence.
application: The Supreme Court first considered Section 426(2)(b), as the case involved an "escaped convict." However, it found that applying this section to a life convict creates a "conundrum," likely because a life sentence does not have a fixed "unexpired" period, making it difficult to determine when a consecutive sentence should start.
Finding Section 426(2)(b) to be unsuitable for the situation, the Court determined that Section 427(2) provided the correct legal framework.
Section 427(2) specifically addresses the scenario of a person already serving a life sentence who receives a subsequent sentence for a term.
Applying this provision, the Court reasoned that the one-year sentence for kidnapping must run concurrently with the pre-existing life sentence for murder.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. was "perfectly in order." It held that the subsequent one-year sentence ran concurrently with the life sentence, and therefore, the appeal by the State was dismissed, upholding the High Court's order to release the detenu.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the continued detention of the detenu after the grant of remission in the first case was illegal.
appellant_arguments: The sentence of imprisonment awarded in the second case (Case No.260/2006) should start running only from the date of grant of remission in the first case, thus justifying the continued detention.
respondent_arguments: The continued detention of the detenu after the grant of remission in the first case was illegal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court's application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. to the case was in order.
appellant_arguments: The High Court's application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. was not in order. (This is inferred from the State's appeal against the High Court's judgment).
respondent_arguments: The High Court's application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. was correct and justified the release of the detenu. (This is inferred as the respondent would be defending the High Court's favorable ruling).

ratio_decidendi.ratio: In law, a life sentence is a sentence for the convict's entire life, and no part of the sentence remains unexpired in the technical sense. Consequently, statutory provisions contingent on a portion of a sentence remaining unexpired, such as Section 426(2)(b) Cr.P.C., cannot be applied to a life convict.
obiter: What remains unexpired of such a sentence is known only to God (if you believe) and to the Government, if there is a policy of remission.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: When a person already serving a life sentence is subsequently convicted and sentenced to another term of life imprisonment, Section 427(2) of the Criminal Procedure Code mandates that the subsequent sentence must run concurrently with the previous one. The grant of remission by the government for the first sentence does not postpone the commencement of the second sentence; both sentences run together from the time the second sentence is imposed.
legal_tests_applied: Direct application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C., which provides that when a person already undergoing a sentence of imprisonment for life is sentenced on a subsequent conviction to imprisonment for a term or imprisonment for life, the subsequent sentence shall run concurrently with such previous sentence.
why_appellant_lost: The appellant's argument that the sentence in the second case should start running only from the date of grant of remission in the first case was directly contrary to the explicit statutory mandate of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C.
The court found that the High Court's application of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C. to the facts of the case was 'perfectly in order', leaving no room for the appellant's interpretation.
why_respondent_won: The detenu's case fell squarely within the conditions of Section 427(2) Cr.P.C., as he was a person 'already undergoing a sentence of imprisonment for life' when he was sentenced to life imprisonment in a subsequent conviction.

Because the two life sentences were required by law to run concurrently, the grant of remission in the first case meant that the effective period of incarceration required for that sentence was complete, and since the second sentence ran alongside it, there was no legal basis for continued detention.
policy_considerations: The court clarified the fundamental nature of a life sentence, stating, 'A life sentence is a sentence for life. What remains unexpired of such a sentence is known only to God... and to the Government, if there is a policy of remission.' This underscores that remission is an executive act of grace that does not alter the judicial sentence's character as lasting for a convict's natural life, which is the conceptual basis for the rule of concurrency in such cases.
